questions.q:
Text C – Small Hospital, Big Hearts (paragraphs 3 and 4)

The work is not glamorous. Volunteers start at seven, scrubbing cages and preparing food that, in the case of the owls, includes defrosted mice. Summer temperatures reach 38 degrees, and the busiest weeks coincide with the hottest, when dehydrated animals arrive by the boxful.
Money is a constant worry. The centre receives no government funding and relies on donations and a small charge for school visits. Last winter a storm tore part of the roof off the owl enclosure, and it took four months to raise enough to repair it.

Identify two challenges the centre faces. [2]
ms: No government funding / relies on donations — money is short (1)
Storm damage (owl enclosure roof) took months to pay for (1)
Extreme summer heat, with most animals arriving in the hottest weeks (1)
Hard, unpleasant, early work (cleaning cages, preparing mice) (1)
questions.model:
1. It has no government funding, so it depends on donations.
2. The busiest period is in extreme summer heat, when many dehydrated animals arrive at once.
questions.tip: Explicit questions: take the information directly from the paragraph, briefly.

questions.q:
TASK: Imagine you are a student who volunteered at the centre for a month last summer. Write a letter to your headteacher suggesting that your school organises a volunteering trip to the centre.
In your letter you should:
• describe the work of the centre and the challenges it faces
• explain what you experienced and learned as a volunteer
• persuade the headteacher of the benefits of the trip for students and for the centre.

Identify two features of form or register your letter should have, given its purpose and audience. [2]
ms: Formal greeting, e.g. “Dear Mr/Ms …” (1)
Appropriate sign-off, e.g. “Yours sincerely” (1)
Formal, polite, respectful register — no slang (1)
Purpose made clear in the opening paragraph (1)
Clear paragraphs following the bullet points (1)
Persuasive but courteous tone suited to a headteacher (1)
questions.model:
1. A formal greeting and sign-off: “Dear Ms Alvarez … Yours sincerely”.
2. A polite, formal register, with the purpose of the letter stated in the first paragraph.
questions.tip: Form and register are part of the writing mark — get them right from the first line.

questions.q:
Text C – Small Hospital, Big Hearts (paragraph 3)

“Summer temperatures reach 38 degrees, and the busiest weeks coincide with the hottest, when dehydrated animals arrive by the boxful.”

TASK: Imagine you are a student who volunteered at the centre for a month last summer. Write a letter to your headteacher suggesting that your school organises a volunteering trip to the centre.
In your letter you should:
• describe the work of the centre and the challenges it faces
• explain what you experienced and learned as a volunteer
• persuade the headteacher of the benefits of the trip for students and for the centre.

Write one or two sentences, in the role of the student, that DEVELOP this detail (draw an inference from it) rather than simply repeating it. [3]
ms: Uses the detail accurately (heat / busiest weeks / dehydrated animals) (1)

Develops it with a reasonable inference, e.g. the centre most needs extra helpers in the summer — exactly when students are on holiday; or staff are exhausted and animals may die without enough hands (1)
Written in role and in a suitable register for the headteacher (1)
questions.model: In the hottest weeks, when dehydrated animals arrive by the boxful, the few staff are stretched to breaking point – which is exactly when our students are on holiday and could make the greatest difference.
questions.tip: Develop = ‘this detail suggests…’ – a logical step beyond the text, not a new story. Marking: No credit for invented events that contradict the text.

questions.q:
Text C – Small Hospital, Big Hearts (magazine article)

On a quiet hillside above the town of Kalamata, a converted farmhouse serves as a hospital for patients who cannot explain what is wrong with them. Last year more than 900 animals were brought through its doors: owls hit by cars, tortoises with cracked shells, hedgehogs tangled in garden netting.
The centre is run by Eleni Markou, a former vet nurse, and a team of volunteers, many of them teenagers. “We teach them everything from the beginning,” Eleni says. “On the first day they are scared to pick up a hedgehog. By the end of the month they are cleaning wounds.”
The work is not glamorous. Volunteers start at seven, scrubbing cages and preparing food that, in the case of the owls, includes defrosted mice. Summer temperatures reach 38 degrees, and the busiest weeks coincide with the hottest, when dehydrated animals arrive by the boxful.
Money is a constant worry. The centre receives no government funding and relies on donations and a small charge for school visits. Last winter a storm tore part of the roof off the owl enclosure, and it took four months to raise enough to repair it.
Yet volunteers keep returning. Sixteen-year-old Nikos, now in his third summer, describes the moment a buzzard he had fed by hand for six weeks was released over the valley. “It circled once,” he says, “as if it was saying goodbye. Then it was just a dot. I have never felt anything like it.”
Not every story ends this way. Around a third of the animals die despite treatment, and Eleni insists volunteers learn to cope with loss. “You cannot save them all,” she says. “But you can make sure none of them suffers alone."

TASK: Imagine you are a student who volunteered at the centre for a month last summer. Write a letter to your headteacher suggesting that your school organises a volunteering trip to the centre.
In your letter you should:
• describe the work of the centre and the challenges it faces
• explain what you experienced and learned as a volunteer
• persuade the headteacher of the benefits of the trip for students and for the centre.

Plan the third bullet point: list two details from the text you could use, and two developed ideas (inferences) that would persuade the headteacher. [4]
ms: Detail: teenagers learn quickly — from being scared of hedgehogs to cleaning wounds within a month (1)
Detail: the centre needs money / relies on donations and charges for school visits (1)
Detail: Nikos’s experience of releasing the buzzard / volunteers keep returning (1)
Developed idea: students gain practical skills, confidence and responsibility — useful for careers in science or veterinary work (1)
Developed idea: the trip’s fee/fundraising directly helps the centre survive (e.g. could pay for repairs like the owl roof) (1)
Developed idea: students learn resilience/empathy by coping with loss (‘none of them suffers alone’) (1)
Developed idea: extra pairs of hands in the busiest, hottest weeks (1)
questions.model:
Details: teenagers go from being scared of hedgehogs to cleaning wounds in a month; the centre relies on donations and charges for school visits.
Developed ideas: students would gain responsibility and confidence that could lead to careers in science or veterinary work; our trip fee and fundraising would help the centre survive emergencies like last winter’s storm damage.
questions.tip: Top-level reading needs both: ideas taken from the text AND ideas developed from them.

In your letter you should:
• describe the work of the centre and the challenges it faces
• explain what you experienced and learned as a volunteer
• persuade the headteacher of the benefits of the trip for students and for the centre.

Write the opening of your letter (about 100 words), covering the first bullet point. [6]
ms: Indicative content:
Formal greeting and clear statement of purpose (proposing a trip)
Describes the centre’s work: treating injured wild animals (owls, tortoises, hedgehogs), over 900 a year, run by a former vet nurse with volunteers
Challenges: no government funding / donations; storm damage to the owl enclosure; extreme heat and busy summer weeks; hard, unglamorous work
Ideas in own words and developed, not copied
Voice of a student who has been there; polite, persuasive register

levels.d: Uses a good range of relevant ideas from the text, partly developed, clearly in role; purpose and register well established; fluent and accurate.
Uses several relevant ideas with some explanation; mostly appropriate register; generally accurate, some lifting.
Few ideas, mostly retold or copied; register or form uncertain; errors may affect clarity.

questions.model:
Dear Ms Alvarez,
I am writing to suggest that our school organises a volunteering trip to the wildlife hospital near Kalamata, where I spent a month last summer. The centre, run by former vet nurse Eleni Markou, treated over 900 injured wild animals last year – owls struck by cars, tortoises with broken shells and hedgehogs caught in netting. Its work is vital, yet it survives without any government money, relying entirely on donations. When a storm wrecked the owl enclosure last winter, it took four months to afford repairs. In summer, when the heat is fiercest, the small team is overwhelmed.
questions.tip: State your purpose in the first sentence — the headteacher should know why you are writing immediately.

Text C – Small Hospital, Big Hearts (magazine article)

TASK: Imagine you are a student who volunteered at the centre for a month last summer. Write a letter to your headteacher suggesting that your school organises a volunteering trip to the centre.
In your letter you should:
• describe the work of the centre and the challenges it faces
• explain what you experienced and learned as a volunteer
• persuade the headteacher of the benefits of the trip for students and for the centre.

Write the section of your letter that covers the second bullet point – what you experienced and learned as a volunteer (about 150 words). [8]
ms: Indicative content:
Early starts at seven; scrubbing cages; preparing food including defrosted mice — developed as what this taught (humility, commitment)
Initial fear of handling animals turning to confidence; learning skills such as cleaning wounds
The emotional high of a release (inspired by Nikos’s buzzard — but should be the student’s own experience developed from the text, not copied)
Coping with loss: a third of animals die; Eleni’s message that none should suffer alone — learned compassion/resilience
Coping with heat and exhaustion; teamwork
Reflective, sincere first-person voice; still appropriate for a headteacher

levels.d: Develops a wide range of ideas from the text with convincing inferences about feelings and learning; consistent, sincere voice in role; well-structured, varied and accurate writing in an appropriate register.
Uses a range of relevant ideas with some development; clear voice and mostly appropriate register; generally accurate.
Some relevant ideas, mainly retold; limited development or reflection; register uneven; some errors.
Few relevant ideas, copied or invented; little sense of role; frequent errors.

questions.model:
My days began at seven, scrubbing cages and preparing meals – including, for the owls, defrosted mice, which tested my stomach on the first morning. On my first day I was too nervous even to lift a hedgehog, yet within weeks I was cleaning wounds under Eleni’s supervision. I learned that patience and routine matter more than glamour.
The most moving moment came when a young owl I had fed by hand for weeks was released over the valley. Watching it shrink to a speck, I understood why volunteers return year after year.
However, not every animal survives; around a third die despite everything. I found this painful, but Eleni taught us that we cannot save them all, only make sure none suffers alone. That lesson in compassion, and in carrying on after disappointment, is something I will keep long after the summer.
questions.tip: Develop feelings and lessons from the text’s details — don’t just list the jobs.
